name: African Grey Parrots
lifetext: African Grey Parrots can live for several decades. Published estimates vary, and individual health, nutrition and care influence longevity. Plan for long-term care rather than relying on a maximum-age claim.
temperament: Observant and responsive parrots with individual differences in confidence and sociability. African Grey Parrots often benefit from predictable routines, patient interaction and meaningful enrichment.
diet: Use a balanced, species-appropriate feeding plan with suitable formulated food and fresh produce. Discuss calcium and overall nutrition with an avian vet, particularly for African greys.
space: Provide room to move, climb and exercise, alongside safe supervised time outside the enclosure. Offer different perch sizes and rotate suitable chew and foraging toys.
noise: Calls and mimicry vary by species and individual. No bird is guaranteed to talk or remain quiet.
fit: A household ready to offer consistent interaction, enrichment and a calm routine.
examples: Congo African greys and Timneh parrots

name: Macaw Parrots
lifetext: Large macaws can live for several decades. Smaller macaw species have different life expectations. Age, nutrition, health and husbandry all influence lifespan; plan for long-term care and a backup caregiver.
temperament: Inquisitive, expressive birds that can enjoy social activity and positive-reinforcement training. Their strong beaks and size call for confident, respectful handling.
diet: Offer suitable formulated food with a varied selection of fresh vegetables and some fruit. Nuts can serve as measured rewards; the right amount depends on species, activity and veterinary advice.
space: Large species need substantial accommodation, strong perches and plenty of safe exercise space. Choose durable enrichment designed for a powerful beak.
noise: Large macaws can produce very loud calls. Consider neighbours and the whole household before choosing one.
fit: Owners with the space, time and resources to meet a large parrot’s daily needs.
examples: Blue-and-gold, scarlet, green-winged and Hahn’s macaws

name: Cockatoo Parrots
lifetext: Lifespan differs markedly between cockatoo species. Published averages and longevity records are not the same thing. These birds require a multi-decade care plan rather than reliance on a single maximum age.
temperament: Often highly expressive and socially demanding. Build healthy independence with foraging and a steady routine as well as time together.
diet: A balanced feeding plan should include suitable formulated food and fresh produce. Keep energy-rich treats measured and review weight and diet with an avian vet.
space: Provide a robust enclosure, safe exercise, appropriate chew materials and regular enrichment. Feather dust is an important consideration when planning the home environment.
noise: Many species have powerful calls. Noise and feather dust can make some homes unsuitable.
fit: A well-prepared household that understands the group’s social demands, noise and long-term needs.
examples: Umbrella, sulphur-crested and Moluccan cockatoos; galahs

name: Amazon Parrots
lifetext: Amazon parrots can be long-lived, but published figures differ between species and populations. Confirm the species and age, and plan for a long-term relationship with ongoing veterinary care.
temperament: Often animated and confident. Body language matters, and behaviour can change with maturity and breeding condition. Individual temperament should guide any match.
diet: Provide suitable formulated food and fresh produce, with measured seeds and nuts rather than a seed-only diet. Balance calorie intake with activity and monitor body condition.
space: Make room for climbing, exercise and robust enrichment. Provide varied perches and opportunities to search for food.
noise: Calls can be loud. Talking ability varies and should never be promised.
fit: Owners willing to learn parrot body language and support exercise, nutrition and consistent routines.
examples: Blue-fronted, yellow-naped and double yellow-headed Amazons

name: Conure Parrots
tag: Small in stature. Full of personality.
lifetext: VCA gives a broad average of 20–35 years for conures. Individual species and birds vary, so this is general guidance rather than a guarantee or an exact estimate for every conure.
temperament: Often active and inquisitive, with a strong interest in exploration. Social preferences and handling tolerance vary by bird.
diet: Suitable pellets and varied fresh produce support balanced nutrition. Avoid relying on seed and nut mixes as the main diet; discuss gradual dietary changes with an avian vet.
space: Allow room for movement and supervised exercise. Choose appropriate bar spacing and small-parrot-safe toys without hazardous loose parts.
noise: Some conures have piercing calls. A smaller body does not mean a quiet companion.
fit: Households ready for an active small parrot with daily enrichment and social interaction.

name: Caique Parrots
lifetext: Caiques are long-term companions. Published husbandry references give differing estimates, with some citing approximately 30–40 years. Treat this as planning guidance, not a promised lifespan.
temperament: Often energetic and exploratory. Give them opportunities to climb, investigate and engage with suitable enrichment while respecting each bird’s boundaries.
diet: Offer a varied, balanced diet with suitable formulated food and fresh produce. Use treats sparingly and keep an eye on body condition.
space: Provide climbing opportunities, safe foot toys and supervised play. Introductions to other birds should be careful and closely managed.
noise: Calls and vocal activity vary. They should not be selected on the assumption that they will be quiet.
fit: People who can offer structured activity and supervise an energetic bird’s exploration.

name: Eclectus Parrots
tag: Two striking palettes. One remarkable group.
lifetext: Animal Diversity Web describes captive life expectations around 23–28 years and an average around 30. Older individuals are reported elsewhere, but exceptional longevity is not a typical-life guarantee.
temperament: Attentive birds with individual preferences for interaction. Avoid assuming that every bird has the same temperament based on sex or appearance.
diet: Discuss an Eclectus-specific nutrition plan with an avian vet, including appropriate fresh produce and formulated food. Avoid routine supplements without professional advice.
space: Provide a roomy enclosure, safe exercise and opportunities to forage. A calm-looking bird still needs movement and mental stimulation.
noise: Eclectus can produce loud calls. Individual vocal patterns and response to household activity vary.
fit: Owners who will pay close attention to diet, daily routine and individual behaviour.
examples: Eclectus species from New Guinea, nearby islands and north-eastern Australia

name: Parakeets & Budgerigars
lifetext: This category spans very different birds. Published examples include around 7–12 years for budgerigars and 25–30 years for Indian ringnecks. Choose the exact species before planning its lifetime care.
temperament: Social, active birds with preferences that vary by species and individual. Small size does not remove the need for companionship, enrichment and gentle handling.
diet: Small parrots need a species-appropriate balance of formulated food, fresh vegetables, some fruit and suitable seeds where appropriate. A seed-only diet is not a balanced plan.
space: Prioritise usable flight space, safe bar spacing and suitable perch diameters. Small birds also need opportunities to exercise and investigate.
noise: Budgies may chatter frequently; other parakeets can have much louder calls. Research the exact species.
fit: Owners looking for a smaller bird while still preparing for meaningful daily care.
examples: Budgerigars, ringnecks, lovebirds, parrotlets and other small parrots
